title: India begins to China-proof its infra push after the TBM shock
summary: India is moving to localise infrastructure machinery after disruptions in supply of tunnel-boring machines (TBMs) from China. The shift aims to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers, speed up delivery of major highway and urban projects, and attract private capital and domestic manufacturing investment to strengthen supply chains and strategic resilience.
content:
India moves to localise infrastructure machinery after China TBM supply disruption.

A disruption in the supply of tunnel-boring machines (TBMs) from China has prompted Indian authorities and industry to reassess dependence on single-source foreign suppliers for critical infrastructure equipment. The event, described in reports as a "TBM shock," has underscored vulnerabilities in project delivery timelines for highways, urban transit and other large-scale works.

The concern comes as India embarks on an ambitious infrastructure expansion. Recent government actions and industry moves referenced alongside the TBM issue include approvals for major highway projects worth tens of thousands of crores, inauguration of the Lucknow-Kanpur Expressway, a focus on decongesting cities such as Varanasi, and private-sector capital mobilisations such as JSW Infrastructure's fund-raising. Financial institutions and development lenders have also announced lending plans to support state infrastructure needs.

Officials and industry leaders are signalling a push to "China-proof" the infrastructure buildout by promoting localisation of machinery and components, diversifying suppliers, and scaling up domestic manufacturing capacity. Measures being discussed or adopted include incentivising local production of heavy equipment, fast-tracking approvals for domestic suppliers, encouraging joint ventures that transfer technology, and using public procurement to create a steady demand signal for Indian manufacturers.

The shift is expected to have multiple effects: it could raise near-term costs or require adjustments in schedules as domestic supply chains develop, but it also offers the potential for long-term gains — deeper industrial capability, more resilient project delivery, and employment growth in manufacturing. Policymakers see private capital playing a larger role in infrastructure investment, and financial institutions have flagged multi-billion-dollar lending windows for state and local projects.

Analysts say success will depend on coherent industrial policy, timely availability of financing, skilling of the workforce, and continued engagement with global partners to secure technology while building local capacity. For now, the TBM disruption has become a catalyst for accelerating efforts to make India's infrastructure programme less exposed to single-country supply shocks and more self-reliant.
